title: TAL research lands as mental health claims reshape group cover pricing
full_text:
TAL has released research on Australians' social habits as part of its Understanding Modern Australia Report, timed for Mental Health Month. The research lands as mental health claims continue to drive up the cost of life cover.
The survey found that 37% of Australians cite tiredness as the main reason they cancel social plans, rising to 45% of women compared with 28% of men. More than seven in 10 said they already make time for activities that support their mental wellbeing. Being close to home was the strongest prompt for following through on plans, cited by 54% of respondents.
Glenn Baird (pictured), head of mental health at TAL, said the findings point to connection as part of looking after mental health.
"Our research shows Australians deeply value their relationships but say they lack the time or resources to connect. At the same time, most people – more than 7 in 10 – are making time for activities that support their mental wellbeing. The opportunity is to bring these things together by treating connection as part of how we look after ourselves," Baird said.
For TAL, prevention research has a clear commercial context. Mental health is now the leading cause of total and permanent disability (TPD) claims, accounting for almost one in three claims paid, according to the Council of Australian Life Insurers (CALI). Insurers paid more than $2.2 billion in retail mental health claims in 2024, almost double the figure from five years earlier. Mental ill health also drove one in five income protection claims, with payouts of $887 million.
Those costs are reaching members. AustralianSuper raised insurance premiums from May 30, 2026, with TPD cover up by an average of 40%, death cover by 20% and income protection by up to 38%. The fund cited a rise in mental health and disability claims among younger members.
Insurers are also redesigning products. TAL launched its TPD Support Option in December 2025, which pays 20% of the sum insured annually, subject to yearly reassessment, rather than a single lump sum. AIA has since launched its own redesigned TPD product.
The regulator has signalled that the product itself is under strain. APRA executive director Jane Magill told the 2026 All Actuaries Summit that the rise in mental health TPD claims was "not just an increase in volume. It's a structural shift that the product's original design was never intended to accommodate."
For advisers, TAL's research is less significant than the pricing environment around it. Clients relying on default cover through super are seeing premiums rise sharply, and the choice between traditional lump-sum TPD and the new staged-payment designs is now a live advice conversation.
